newsitem.title: FRANCE: French, Germans clash on economics, NATO.
newsitem.headline: French, Germans clash on economics, NATO.

text.p: French and German politicians clashed on economic policies and NATO on Tuesday in an unusually frank baring of differences between Europe's central allies over the future of the European Union.

Francois Hollande, interim leader of France's newly-elected governing Socialist party, accused Germany of having gone back on past agreements to launch job-creating public works projects and of being less concerned about unemployment than Paris.

Bonn had distorted the purpose of the planned single European currency by harping on strict adherence to the economic criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), he told a Paris conference on problems in Franco-German relations.
He renewed French calls for a political counterweight to the future independent European Central Bank.

Christian Democratic EU expert Karl Lamers, a close associate of Chancellor Helmut Kohl, retorted that Germany was just as concerned as France about fighting unemployment but differed on how to do it.
Contradicting the ideas of France's left-wing government, he called for flexible labour markets and reform of overstrained welfare systems.

Publicly-funded infrastructure programmes would put Europe back into a vicious circle of mounting debt and high interest rates, Lamers argued. "The recipes of the past are clearly not the right ones," he said.
Lamers backed the idea of a political body to coordinate EU economic policies but said the problem was agreeing on the content of those policies.
German opposition Social Democrat (SPD) Ingomar Hauchler also took issue with Hollande, questioning "whether we really need old, state-funded Keynesian infrastructure programmes."
Lamers and SPD foreign affairs spokesman Karsten Voigt also criticised France's decision to halt its return to the NATO defence alliance's integrated military command.
Both men said the French decision, taken after the United States refused to hand over NATO's key southern command to a European, would make it harder to build a European defence identity.

"The fact that France is staying out of integration won't increase French influence and will make us more dependent on the United States and make it more difficult to organise a European pillar in NATO," Voigt told the conference.

French National Assembly speaker Laurent Fabius, acknowledging the serious problems facing Europe's central "couple", urged the heads of the German and French governments to address each other's parliaments to revive a friendship soured by differences over the single European currency.
Fabius, a former Socialist premier, told the seminar that Kohl should address the French National Assembly and French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin the Bundestag in an effort to restore frayed ties.

He said the Franco-German duo, which has been the driving force of European unity, was going through "very serious difficulties" after last month's failed bilateral summit in the French town of Poitiers and an EU summit in Amsterdam.
"This is a serious and unprecedented situation that (former European Commission president) Jacques Delors rightly described as a fiasco," he said.

"In order to emerge from this spiral of misunderstanding, the first thing to do is to repair the frayed threads at the top. Let (Kohl and Jospin) explain themselves and learn to know each other better."

Fabius added: "Too much is at stake in the Franco-German relationship for it to be taken for granted, as it is going through serious problems that are increasingly apparent despite ritual meetings between the two countries' leaders."
